name: Hippocampal Relational Binding and Encoding
higher_order_principle: The hippocampus transforms experience into memory through relational binding — creating conjunctive representations that link the what (item information from LEC/perirhinal), where (spatial context from MEC/parahippocampal), and when (temporal context from MEC time cells) of an experience. Encoding strength is driven by prediction error (CA1 mismatch detection), modulated by emotional arousal (amygdala), schema congruence (vmPFC), and attention (prefrontal gating). Encoding that generates PE produces stronger, more durable memory traces than encoding that confirms predictions.

causal_links.key_evidence: Davachi, 2006; Kumaran & Maguire, 2006; Chen et al., 2015

parameters.mechanism: CA1 receives current input (entorhinal) and retrieved pattern (CA3). Mismatch between them = PE = encoding signal.
parameters.high_PE: strongly engages encoding — novel, surprising, schema-violating information
parameters.low_PE: weakly engages encoding — familiar, expected, schema-congruent information
parameters.educational_implication: PASSIVE re-exposure generates LOW PE → POOR encoding. ACTIVE prediction/generation generates HIGH PE → STRONG encoding.

inputs.where: MEC → parahippocampal → spatial context, scene layout
inputs.when: MEC time cells → temporal context, sequence position

parameters.output: conjunctive episodic trace binding all elements
parameters.critical_property: trace is CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — retrieval requires matching context cues

parameters.mechanism: amygdala → hippocampus direct projections enhance LTP

inverted_U.moderate_arousal: OPTIMAL encoding (curiosity, mild surprise, personal relevance)
inverted_U.high_arousal: impaired HIPPOCAMPAL encoding but enhanced AMYGDALA encoding (fragmented, emotional-gist memory — the test anxiety pattern)

parameters.educational_implication: moderate emotional engagement without threat = optimal

causal_links.key_evidence: van Kesteren et al., 2012; Tse et al., 2007

parameters.schema_congruent: vmPFC detects fit → partial hippocampal bypass → fast neocortical integration → gist-like memory (good for facts, weak for details)
parameters.schema_incongruent: vmPFC detects violation → STRONG hippocampal encoding (PE signal) → detailed episodic trace (good for details, memorable because surprising)
parameters.schema_irrelevant: no schema activated → weak encoding on all pathways → requires brute-force repetition or artificial scaffolding

parameters.mechanism: MEC time cells provide slowly drifting context signal. Items encoded close in time share similar context → become associated. Items encoded far apart in time have different contexts → more independent.

educational_implication.spacing: different temporal contexts → more retrieval routes → better retention
educational_implication.interleaving: different category items in each temporal context → forces content-based rather than context-based discrimination

scope_conditions: Encoding requires ATTENTION — hippocampal encoding is sharply reduced when attention is divided (Uncapher & Rugg, 2005). Distracted encoding (multitasking, phone use during study) dramatically impairs memory formation.
Encoding is enhanced by GENERATION — producing an answer (even an incorrect one) generates stronger PE than passively receiving the answer.
Encoding is enhanced by ELABORATION — connecting new information to existing knowledge creates more retrieval routes, even when schema is weak.
Age modulates encoding: hippocampal encoding is robust from early childhood; prefrontal control of encoding (strategic encoding) matures slowly through adolescence.
moderators: sleep_status (sleep deprivation impairs initial encoding, not just consolidation)
stress_level (acute stress shifts processing from hippocampal to striatal/amygdala)

interactions.description: Both rely on prediction error. T1 is perceptual/cortical PE; E1 is mnemonic/hippocampal PE. They often co-occur.
During encoding, DMN must often be SUPPRESSED (if externally focused). During subsequent rest, DMN must be ACTIVE for replay (E5).
High threat (T5) impairs hippocampal encoding (E1) via cortisol/catecholamine overdose, shifting to amygdala-only encoding.

key_references: Davachi, L. (2006). Item, context and relational episodic encoding in humans. Current Opinion in Neurobiology
Davachi, L., & DuBrow, S. (2015). How the hippocampus preserves order. Trends in Cognitive Sciences
Eichenbaum, H. (2000). A cortical-hippocampal system for declarative memory. Nature Reviews Neuroscience
van Kesteren, M. T. R., et al. (2012). How schema and novelty augment memory formation. Trends in Neurosciences
Kumaran, D., & Maguire, E. A. (2006). An unexpected sequence of events: Mismatch detection in the human hippocampus. PLoS Biology
